q: Heat is the form of energy that can be transferred from one system to another as a result of temperature difference.
e: This is the exact definition of heat provided in the textbook.

q: Heat is the form of energy that can be transferred from one system to another as a result of pressure difference.
e: Heat is transferred as a result of temperature difference, not pressure difference.

q: Heat transfer and thermodynamics are two complementary branches of science.
e: The textbook introduces them as complementary branches of science.

q: Heat transfer and thermodynamics are two unrelated branches of science.
e: The text states they are complementary, not unrelated.

q: Heat transfer is a discipline of thermal engineering that concerns the generation, use, conversion, and exchange of thermal energy between systems.
e: This is the exact definition of heat transfer from the text.

q: Thermodynamics deals with equilibrium states by outlining the relationship between energy and work.
e: This accurately reflects the textbook's definition of thermodynamics.

q: Thermodynamics deals with non-equilibrium states by outlining the relationship between energy and work.
e: Thermodynamics deals with equilibrium states, not non-equilibrium states.

q: One of the basic requirements for heat transfer is the presence of a temperature difference.
e: A temperature difference is required for net heat transfer to occur.

q: There can be no net heat transfer between two systems that are at the same temperature.
e: Systems at the same temperature are in thermal equilibrium, meaning no net heat transfer.

q: There can be maximum net heat transfer between two systems that are at the same temperature.
e: There is no net heat transfer between systems at the same temperature.

q: There are three basic ways of heat transfer; namely, heat conduction, heat convection and heat radiation.
e: These are the three fundamental modes of heat transfer listed in the text.

q: In fluids, heat is mainly transferred by convection, in which the motion of the fluid itself carries heat from one place to another.
e: This is the exact mechanism of heat convection described in the textbook.

q: In fluids, heat is mainly transferred by conduction, in which the motion of the fluid itself carries heat from one place to another.
e: Heat carried by the motion of the fluid itself is convection, not conduction.

q: In solid, heat is transferred by conduction process in which heat energy is transferred among the adjacent parts of the material without the motion of the material itself.
e: This correctly defines heat conduction in solids.

q: The third way to transfer heat energy is by radiation process in the form of electromagnetic waves.
e: Thermal radiation transfers energy via electromagnetic waves.

q: The third way to transfer heat energy is by radiation process in the form of mechanical waves.
e: Radiation transfers heat via electromagnetic waves, not mechanical waves.

q: The individual parts of a medium do not move whole in heat conduction.
e: In conduction, energy is transferred without the bulk movement of the medium.

q: Heat energy is transferred by successive distribution among the adjacent parts in heat conduction.
e: This describes the microscopic mechanism of heat conduction.

q: When heat is transferred via conduction, heat energy is transferred internally by vibrations of atoms and molecules.
e: Atomic and molecular vibrations are responsible for internal heat transfer in conduction.

q: When heat is transferred via conduction, heat energy is transferred internally by the flow of free protons.
e: Heat is transferred by vibrations of atoms/molecules and free electrons, not free protons.

q: Metals have many free electrons.
e: The presence of free electrons is a key characteristic of metals.

q: Since these free electrons can carry heat, metals are generally very good conductors of heat.
e: Free electrons significantly enhance the thermal conductivity of metals.

q: Since these free electrons can carry heat, metals are generally very poor conductors of heat.
e: Free electrons make metals very good conductors, not poor conductors.

q: The rate of heat conduction through a material of cross-sectional area $A$ is proportional to the temperature difference $\Delta T$.
e: This is a core principle of Fourier's law of heat conduction.

q: The rate of heat conduction through a material of cross-sectional area $A$ is inversely proportional to the temperature difference $\Delta T$.
e: The rate of heat conduction is directly proportional to the temperature difference.

q: The rate of heat conduction through a material is inversely proportional to the thickness $l$ of the material.
e: Thicker materials reduce the rate of heat conduction.

q: The heat transfer or conduction rate $H$ is $H = kA \frac{T_2 - T_1}{l}$.
e: This is the exact mathematical formula for heat conduction rate provided in the text.

q: In the heat conduction formula, $k$ is the thermal conductivity of the material, which is a measure of the ability of a material to conduct heat.
e: This is the correct definition of the thermal conductivity constant $k$.

q: In SI units, $k$ is watt per metre per kelvin ($W m^{-1} K^{-1}$).
e: This is the correct SI unit for thermal conductivity.

q: In SI units, $k$ is watt per metre squared per kelvin ($W m^{-2} K^{-1}$).
e: The SI unit for thermal conductivity is $W m^{-1} K^{-1}$, not $W m^{-2} K^{-1}$.

q: The ratio $\frac{T_2 - T_1}{l}$ is called temperature gradient.
e: This ratio defines the temperature gradient in the context of heat conduction.

q: This mathematical model of heat conduction was first formulated by the French physicist Jean Baptiste Joseph Fourier in his Fourier's law of heat conduction.
e: Fourier's law is named after the French physicist who formulated it.

q: Fourier's law of heat conduction states that the rate of heat flow per unit area (heat flux density) is proportional to the magnitude of temperature gradient.
e: This is the formal statement of Fourier's law of heat conduction.

q: Fourier's law of heat conduction states that the rate of heat flow per unit area is inversely proportional to the magnitude of temperature gradient.
e: Heat flux density is directly proportional to the temperature gradient.

q: In Fourier's law, the negative sign indicates that temperature $T$ must decrease as distance $x$ increases.
e: The negative sign accounts for heat flowing from higher to lower temperatures.

q: In the SI units, heat flux density is watt per metre squared ($W m^{-2}$) and heat current is watt ($W$).
e: These are the correct SI units for heat flux density and heat current respectively.

q: The thermal conductivity of a material can be defined as the rate of heat transfer per unit area per unit temperature gradient.
e: This is the formal definition of thermal conductivity derived from Fourier's law.

q: A high value for thermal conductivity indicates that the material is a poor thermal conductor or thermal insulator.
e: A high value indicates a good thermal conductor, while a low value indicates an insulator.

q: A low value for thermal conductivity indicates that the material is a poor thermal conductor or thermal insulator.
e: Materials with low thermal conductivity resist heat flow, acting as insulators.

q: Materials such as copper and silver that are good electric conductors are also good heat conductors, and have high values of thermal conductivity.
e: Good electrical conductors typically have high thermal conductivity due to free electrons.

q: Materials such as rubber, wood, and styrofoam are poor conductors of heat and have low conductivity values.
e: These materials are classic examples of thermal insulators with low $k$ values.

q: Heat convection is the flow of heat through a fluid from places of higher temperature to places of lower temperature by movement of the fluid itself.
e: This is the exact textbook definition of heat convection.

q: Heat convection is the flow of heat through a solid from places of higher temperature to places of lower temperature by movement of the material itself.
e: Convection occurs in fluids (liquids and gases), not solids.

q: In heat convection, the transfer of energy occurs between an object and its environment due to fluid motion.
e: Fluid motion is the primary driver of energy transfer in convection.

q: Convection currents are set up in the fluid because the hotter part of the fluid is not as dense as the cooler part.
e: Thermal expansion makes hotter fluid less dense, driving convection currents.

q: Convection currents are set up in the fluid because the hotter part of the fluid is denser than the cooler part.
e: Hotter fluid is less dense, not denser, than the cooler fluid.

q: There is an upward buoyant force on the hotter fluid, making it rise while the cooler and denser fluid sinks.
e: Buoyancy drives the physical movement of fluid in natural convection.

q: Convection occurs only in a liquid or a gas, never in a solid.
e: Convection requires fluid motion, which cannot happen in solids.

q: Convection occurs in solids, liquids, and gases equally.
e: Convection never occurs in solids.

q: Buoyant force is what drives natural convection.
e: Density differences leading to buoyant forces are the mechanism for natural convection.

q: The basic equation for the rate of convection heat transfer is known as Newton's law of cooling.
e: Newton's law of cooling provides the mathematical model for convection heat transfer rate.

q: The basic equation for the rate of convection heat transfer is known as Fourier's law of cooling.
e: Fourier's law applies to conduction, while Newton's law of cooling applies to convection.

q: In Newton's law of cooling, $q$ is the convective heat transfer coefficient.
e: The text uses $q$ to denote the convective heat transfer coefficient.

q: When $T_2 > T_1$ in convection, heat is gained by the object and $H$ is positive.
e: A hotter surrounding fluid transfers heat to the object, making the heat transfer rate positive.

q: When $T_2 < T_1$ in convection, heat is gained by the object and $H$ is positive.
e: When the surrounding fluid is cooler ($T_2 < T_1$), heat is lost by the object and $H$ is negative.

q: Heat radiation is a transfer of heat that does not require a material medium.
e: Radiation can travel through a vacuum, unlike conduction and convection.

q: Heat radiation is a transfer of heat that strictly requires a dense material medium.
e: Radiation does not require any material medium.

q: Heat is transferred by thermal radiation which are electromagnetic waves that pass through a medium or even vacuum.
e: Thermal radiation consists of electromagnetic waves.

q: Energy transfer by radiation is the fastest (at the speed of light) and it suffers no attenuation in a vacuum.
e: Electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light and do not attenuate in a vacuum.

q: Energy transfer by radiation suffers maximum attenuation in a vacuum.
e: Radiation suffers no attenuation in a vacuum.

q: Thermal radiation is the form of radiation emitted by bodies because of their temperature.
e: Temperature is the sole cause of thermal radiation emission.

q: All bodies at a temperature above absolute zero emit thermal radiation.
e: Any object above $0 K$ emits some form of thermal radiation.

q: Only bodies at a temperature below absolute zero emit thermal radiation.
e: Bodies above absolute zero emit thermal radiation; nothing can be below absolute zero.

q: Thermal radiation differs from other forms of electromagnetic radiation such as X-rays, gamma rays, microwave and radio wave that are not related to temperature.
e: Thermal radiation is specifically tied to the temperature of the emitting body.

q: Radiation is mostly considered to be a surface phenomenon for solids that are opaque to thermal radiation.
e: Opaque solids absorb and emit thermal radiation primarily at their surfaces.

q: Radiation is mostly considered to be a bulk volume phenomenon for solids that are opaque to thermal radiation.
e: For opaque solids, radiation is a surface phenomenon, not a bulk volume one.

q: If an object has a good rate of emission of radiation, then it also has a good rate of absorption.
e: Good emitters are inherently good absorbers of radiation.

q: The object which can absorb all the electromagnetic radiations falling upon it is called a blackbody.
e: A blackbody is defined as a perfect absorber of all incident radiation.

q: The object which can reflect all the electromagnetic radiations falling upon it is called a blackbody.
e: A blackbody absorbs all incident radiation; it does not reflect it.

q: The blackbody is not only a perfect absorber but also a best emitter of radiation.
e: A blackbody represents the theoretical maximum for both absorption and emission.

q: The total emissive power is defined as the total radiant energy of different wavelengths emitted from unit area of a surface of a body in one second.
e: This is the exact textbook definition of total emissive power.

q: The total emissive power of a blackbody is directly proportional to the fourth power of absolute temperature.
e: This relationship is the core of the Stefan-Boltzmann law.

q: The total emissive power of a blackbody is directly proportional to the square of absolute temperature.
e: It is proportional to the fourth power, not the square, of the absolute temperature.

q: The equation $e_0 = \sigma T^4$ is known as Stefan-Boltzmann's law.
e: This mathematical expression represents the Stefan-Boltzmann law for a blackbody.

q: The radiation emitted by all real surfaces is less than the radiation emitted by a blackbody at the same temperature.
e: Real surfaces have an emissivity less than 1, making them emit less than a perfect blackbody.

q: The radiation emitted by all real surfaces is greater than the radiation emitted by a blackbody at the same temperature.
e: No real surface can emit more radiation than a blackbody at the same temperature.

q: Emissivity is defined as the ratio of the total emissive power of an object to that of the blackbody, at the same temperature and wavelength.
e: This is the formal definition of emissivity.

q: Emissivity of an object depends to a large extent on how shiny it is.
e: Surface properties like shininess heavily influence an object's emissivity.

q: A black object is a good absorber and a good radiator whose emissivity is close to 1.
e: Dark, black surfaces approximate blackbody behavior with high emissivity.

q: A white, clear, or silver coated object is a poor absorber and a poor radiator whose emissivity is close to 1.
e: Shiny or silver-coated objects have an emissivity much less than 1.

q: The net energy change is simply the difference between the radiated energy and the absorbed energy.
e: Net radiation heat transfer is calculated by subtracting absorbed energy from radiated energy.

q: Thermodynamics is the study of systems involving energy in the form of heat and work.
e: This is the foundational definition of thermodynamics provided in the text.

q: Thermodynamics is the study of systems involving energy exclusively in the form of mechanical kinetic energy.
e: Thermodynamics specifically focuses on energy in the form of heat and work.

q: Thermal equilibrium is an important concept in thermodynamics.
e: Thermal equilibrium is central to defining temperature and thermodynamic states.

q: When two systems are in thermal equilibrium, there is no net heat transfer between them.
e: Lack of net heat transfer is the defining characteristic of thermal equilibrium.

q: When two systems are in thermal equilibrium, there is maximum net heat transfer between them.
e: There is zero net heat transfer between systems in thermal equilibrium.

q: Systems at the same temperature will be in thermal equilibrium with each other.
e: Equal temperature is the condition required for thermal equilibrium.

q: The zeroth law of thermodynamics states that when two objects are separately in thermodynamic equilibrium with a third object, they all are in thermodynamic equilibrium with each other.
e: This is the exact statement of the Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics.

q: The first law of thermodynamics is an application of the conservation energy for heat and thermodynamic processes.
e: The First Law is essentially the principle of conservation of energy applied to thermal systems.

q: The first law of thermodynamics relates the change in internal energy of a system to heat added and the work done by the system.
e: This correctly summarizes the variables involved in the First Law.

q: The change in internal energy $\Delta U$ of a system is equal to the net heat flow $Q$ into the system minus the total work $W$ done by the system.
e: This is the standard mathematical formulation of the First Law: $\Delta U = Q - W$.

q: The change in internal energy $\Delta U$ of a system is equal to the net heat flow $Q$ into the system plus the total work $W$ done by the system.
e: The correct formula is $\Delta U = Q - W$, where work done by the system is subtracted.

q: In the first law of thermodynamics, $Q$ is positive if heat is added to the system, and negative if heat is removed.
e: This is the standard sign convention for heat flow in thermodynamics.

q: In the first law of thermodynamics, $W$ is positive if work is done on the system, and negative if work is done by the system.
e: The textbook states $W$ is positive if work is done BY the system, and negative if done ON the system.

q: The internal energy $U$ of a system is defined as the sum of the energies of all the constituent particles.
e: This is the microscopic definition of macroscopic internal energy.

q: The internal energy of ideal gases depends only on temperature, not on volume or pressure.
e: For an ideal gas, internal energy is a function of temperature alone.

q: The internal energy of ideal gases depends only on volume and pressure, not on temperature.
e: Internal energy of an ideal gas depends strictly on its temperature.

q: Internal energy of an ideal gas is directly proportional to the absolute temperature.
e: As absolute temperature increases, the internal energy of an ideal gas increases proportionally.

q: Heat transfer and work are both energy in transit.
e: Heat and work represent energy moving across system boundaries.

q: Heat transfer and work are both stored as such in a system.
e: Neither heat nor work is stored in a system; only internal energy is stored.

q: Internal energy is a form of energy completely different from either heat or work.
e: Internal energy is a state property, whereas heat and work are path-dependent transfer mechanisms.

q: A thermodynamic process may be defined as a change from one equilibrium state of a system to another.
e: This is the standard definition of a thermodynamic process.

q: In thermodynamics, a quasi-static process is a thermodynamic process that happens slowly enough for the system to remain in internal physical thermodynamic equilibrium.
e: Quasi-static processes are idealized as being infinitely slow to maintain equilibrium.

q: In thermodynamics, a quasi-static process is a thermodynamic process that happens very rapidly to prevent the system from remaining in internal physical thermodynamic equilibrium.
e: A quasi-static process happens slowly specifically to maintain internal equilibrium.

q: An isobaric process occurs at constant pressure.
e: The prefix 'iso-baric' denotes constant pressure.

q: An isobaric process occurs at constant volume.
e: An isobaric process occurs at constant pressure; constant volume is an isochoric process.

q: The work done by the system in an isobaric process is simply the pressure multiplied by the change in volume.
e: The formula for work in an isobaric process is $W = p \Delta V$.

q: An isochoric process occurs at constant volume.
e: The prefix 'iso-choric' denotes constant volume.

q: When the volume of a thermodynamic system is constant, no work is done by the system because $W = p \Delta V = 0$.
e: Since there is no change in volume ($\Delta V = 0$), boundary work is zero.

q: According to the first law, in an isochoric process, the change in internal energy must equal any heat flowing into or out of the system.
e: Since $W=0$, the First Law ($\Delta U = Q - W$) simplifies to $\Delta U = Q$.

q: An isothermal process occurs at a constant temperature.
e: The prefix 'iso-thermal' denotes constant temperature.

q: For an ideal gas, internal energy $U$ is only a function of the volume.
e: For an ideal gas, internal energy is only a function of temperature.

q: Internal energy is constant; therefore, $\Delta U$ is equal to zero for an isothermal process.
e: Because temperature is constant in an isothermal process for an ideal gas, $\Delta U = 0$.

q: Since $\Delta U = 0$, according to the first law, $W = Q$ for an isothermal process.
e: With no change in internal energy, all heat added to the system is converted into work done by the system.

q: In an adiabatic process, there is no heat transfer into or out of the system, i.e., $Q = 0$.
e: An adiabatic process is defined by the absence of heat exchange.

q: In an adiabatic process, there is maximum heat transfer into or out of the system.
e: An adiabatic process involves zero heat transfer.

q: The first law of thermodynamics $\Delta U = Q - W$ is thus reduced to $\Delta U = -W$ for an adiabatic process.
e: Substituting $Q = 0$ into the First Law yields $\Delta U = -W$.

q: An adiabatic process can be done by enclosing the system in a thermal insulator.
e: Thermal insulation prevents heat transfer, creating an adiabatic boundary.

q: Heat engine is a system that converts heat to mechanical energy, which can then be used to do mechanical work.
e: This is the primary function and definition of a heat engine.

q: Heat engine is a system that converts mechanical energy to heat energy, which can then be used to do thermal work.
e: A heat engine converts heat into mechanical work, not the reverse.

q: A series of processes in which a system is brought back to its initial state is called a cycle.
e: This is the exact definition of a thermodynamic cycle.

q: Thermal efficiency for a heat engine is the ratio of work output to heat input.
e: Efficiency measures how much of the input heat is successfully converted to useful work.

q: Thermal efficiency for a heat engine is the ratio of heat input to work output.
e: Efficiency is the ratio of work output to heat input, not the inverse.

q: Applying the first law of thermodynamic to one complete cycle, remembering that there is no net change of internal energy ($\Delta U = 0$), we get, $Q_H - Q_C = W$.
e: Over a complete cycle, the net heat added equals the net work done.

q: The transformation of heat into work is usually accomplished in practice by two general types of engine; the internal combustion engine and the steam engine.
e: These are the two primary practical categories of heat engines mentioned in the text.

q: In the gasoline engines, the combustion of the gasoline and air takes place explosively by an electric spark.
e: Spark ignition is the defining characteristic of a standard gasoline engine.

q: In the gasoline engines, the combustion of the gasoline and air takes place slowly by compression heat alone.
e: Ignition by compression heat alone describes a diesel engine, not a gasoline engine.

q: The cycle involves the performance of six processes, of which four require motion of the piston and are called strokes.
e: This accurately describes the structure of the four-stroke engine cycle.

q: Intake stroke: A mixture of gasoline vapour and air is drawn into the cylinder by the suction stroke of the piston.
e: This is the correct description of the intake stroke in a gasoline engine.

q: Compression stroke: The mixture of gasoline vapour and air is compressed until its pressure and temperature rise considerably.
e: Compression increases both the pressure and temperature of the fuel-air mixture.

q: Explosion: Combustion of the hot mixture is caused to take place very rapidly by an electric spark.
e: The spark plug initiates the rapid combustion event known as the explosion or power stroke ignition.

q: Power stroke: The hot combustion products expand and push the piston out, thus suffering a drop in pressure and temperature.
e: Expansion of gases does work on the piston, lowering the gas pressure and temperature.

q: Valve exhaust: The combustion products at the end of the power stroke are still at a higher pressure and temperature than the outside.
e: Opening the exhaust valve releases the high-pressure residual gases.

q: Exhaust stroke: The piston pushes almost all the remaining combustion products out of the cylinder.
e: The upward movement of the piston clears the cylinder for the next cycle.

q: The diesel engine operates on either a two-stroke or four-stroke cycle.
e: Diesel engines can be designed to operate using either cycle configuration.

q: Unlike the spark-ignition gasoline engine, the diesel engine induces only air into the combustion chamber on its intake stroke.
e: Diesel engines compress pure air; fuel is injected later in the cycle.

q: Unlike the spark-ignition gasoline engine, the diesel engine induces a mixture of fuel and air into the combustion chamber on its intake stroke.
e: Diesel engines induce only air on the intake stroke, not a fuel-air mixture.

q: Diesel fuel is sprayed into the cylinder by the injector and immediately ignites because of the heat and pressure inside the cylinder.
e: Compression ignition occurs spontaneously due to the high temperature of the compressed air.

q: In 1824, Nicolas Leonard Sadi Carnot described a hypothetical engine known as Carnot engine.
e: Sadi Carnot introduced this theoretical concept in 1824.

q: Carnot engine is a heat engine operates on an ideal reversible cycle (Carnot cycle) between two heat reservoirs.
e: The Carnot cycle is entirely composed of ideal reversible processes.

q: Carnot engine is a heat engine operates on an irreversible cycle between two heat reservoirs.
e: The Carnot engine operates on an ideal reversible cycle, not an irreversible one.

q: Carnot engine sets an upper limit on the efficiency of all other real engines.
e: No real engine can exceed the theoretical maximum efficiency of a Carnot engine.

q: All real engines are less efficient than Carnot engine because they do not operate through a reversible cycle.
e: Irreversibilities like friction and rapid expansion reduce the efficiency of real engines.

q: All real engines are more efficient than Carnot engine because they operate through a reversible cycle.
e: Real engines are less efficient than the Carnot engine and operate irreversibly.

q: In a reversible process, the system undergoing the process can be returned to its initial condition along the same path on the p-V diagram.
e: This is a key defining characteristic of a thermodynamically reversible process.

q: The most important condition for a process to be reversible in thermodynamics is that the process should be carried out infinitesimally slowly.
e: Infinitely slow execution ensures the system remains in continuous equilibrium.

q: The most important condition for a process to be reversible in thermodynamics is that the process should be carried out as rapidly as possible.
e: Rapid processes create disequilibrium and are inherently irreversible.

q: The Carnot cycle consists of four reversible processes; two isothermal processes and two adiabatic processes.
e: These four specific processes make up the complete Carnot cycle.

q: The Carnot cycle consists of four reversible processes; two isobaric processes and two isochoric processes.
e: The Carnot cycle uses isothermal and adiabatic processes, not isobaric and isochoric.

q: Carnot's theorem states that no engine operating between two heat reservoirs can be more efficient than a Carnot engine operating between the same reservoirs.
e: This is the formal statement of Carnot's theorem.

q: Carnot's theorem states that any engine operating between two heat reservoirs can be more efficient than a Carnot engine operating between the same reservoirs.
e: Carnot's theorem explicitly states that no engine can be more efficient than the Carnot engine.

q: A corollary to Carnot's theorem states that all reversible engines operating between the same heat reservoirs are equally efficient.
e: Any completely reversible engine will achieve the exact same maximum Carnot efficiency.

q: A corollary to Carnot's theorem states that all reversible engines operating between the same heat reservoirs have different efficiencies.
e: All reversible engines operating between the same reservoirs have the exact same efficiency.
